#4027. Heartopia shows off My Little Pony collaboration, and there's a pre-launch event to hold you over

Heartopia’s My Little Pony collaboration is close, and the pre-launch event has already kicked off.

Heartopia has officially shared initial details about its first-ever collaboration event. The game, which launched a month ago to great success on mobile, as well as Steam on PC, has already been a staple among fans of Animal Crossing and The Sims.

Things are kicking into gear, it seems, because the game is already about to host its first collaboration event, and it is with My Little Pony.

The Heartopia X My Little Pony event officially begins on February 14, but a pre-launch login event is now live through the actual collaboration’s start. The limited-time event offers players sign-in puzzles every day that will unlock time-limited Exhibition Passes.

The first actual piece of My Little Pony-themed content can be yours if you complete all puzzles, as that gets you a limited edition costume for your pet, based on the show’s Spike. The event itself, which will be available until March 15, brings My Little Pony’s Tree of Harmony into the world of Heartopia.

The ponies need your help to Wield Elements of Harmony so they can reawaken the tree, and bring it back to Equestria. In gameplay terms, you’re going to want to perform daily sensing at the tree in order to earn three of the six Elements of Harmony: Honesty, Generosity, Loyalty, Kindness, Laughter, and Magic.

The more you do this, the more the tree’s Energy goes up, and the more rewards and resources you stand to earn. Even more time-limited Exhibition Passes, and Moonlight Crystals can be earned as you water the tree.

Badge Pull Tokens are your big reward, which is what you’re actually going to use to get the special Pony Series badges. You’ll earn ten time-limited Exhibition Passes each time you complete one of the three sets of Pony Series badges. Collect all three and you’ll earn Town Collaboration Series badges.

Heartopia is a free-to-play game, so you know there is a Gacha component to this event. Expect six non-replacement Gacha Pools that each map to one member of My Little Pony’s Mane Six. Within each pool, you’ll be able to earn five outfit pieces, and one vehicle.

If any of that sounds interesting, definitely log in now to play the pre-launch event, which should hold you over until the proper show kicks off Saturday. If you’re already enjoying Heartopia, you likely want to learn about Onsen Egg Promise locations, Fish locations, and Bug locations - all of which can be found at those links.

We also recently updated our guides on how to catch Frostspore fish - and if you’re into cooking, how to obtain every recipe and variant. If you haven’t already, definitely see if you missed any of these Heartopia codes, too.

#4026. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 30, 2026

Welcome to Devil's Night, the night before Halloween, where video games are best served scary. After tomorrow night – Halloween proper – no more scary video games allowed. At least not until mid-September, 2027. I'm sorry, I don't make the rules. Below you will find our weekend gaming recommendations (which is actually surprisingly light on scary games – apologies), but before that, here are some of the biggest stories of the week.

Phantom Blade Zero is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and it’s certainly one of the most impressive to watch. Beijing-based developer S-Game uses China’s Wuxia brand of action (which was actually banned for some time during the 20th Century by the country’s government) to create a stylish, fluid, and hyper-engaging combat system. It will constantly leave you in awe that action combat can look this good. But looks aren’t everything. Fortunately, Phantom Blade Zero delivers on all fronts, with weapon mechanics so detailed that picking up a new blade can feel like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. The story won’t blow your socks off, but it’s certainly engaging and enticing enough to bring you through Phantom Blade Zero’s 40 or so hours of content. If you’re not interested in the “perfect ending,” which is the only satisfactory one in my opinion, you can complete the game in less than 30 hours. S-Game mixes high-octane combat with sprawling and rewarding exploration to create a must-play during this already busy season of games. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Phantom Blade Zero review, and if you are hopping in this weekend, be sure to check out my list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks I wish I knew before starting it.

If you have any fond memories of IllFonic’s ill-fated Friday the 13th: The Game as I do, you simply must play the studio’s latest, Halloween: The Game. It is essentially Friday the 13th with Michael Myers instead of Jason, but with a decade of lessons learned from the team’s teeth carving in other horror properties and games. You’re either Michael or a citizen; the former wants to kill you and all the NPCs in various suburban maps, while the latter must rescue as many NPCs as possible while staying alive themselves. It’s that classic cat-and-mouse formula IllFonic is the master of, but with all the style, substance, and synths of John Carpenter’s Halloween masterpiece. Plus, Halloween: The Game features IllFonic’s first crack at a single-player campaign, and while it’s largely a tutorial for playing as Michael, if you’re a Halloween mega-fan like me, it’s worth checking out if only to take part in some of the film’s most iconic kills. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Halloween: The Game review here, and if you’re hopping in this weekend, there’s a new map, additional Halloween-themed cosmetics to unlock, and more waiting for you.

Overwatch is in the midst of its Halloween event, which have always historically been pretty interesting. This year it's Mystery Madness: Graveyard Games. In it, you begin by picking one of three characters in a random role. And then, as the game progresses, you choose perks that upgrade, alter, or completely change what your character can do. It can get really chaotic where by round three characters like Orisa might be three times her normal size or Torbjorn might have placed a giant turret on Mercy's making her a flying death machine. There are also Halloween skins, as well.

Tom the Postgirl is an odd little adventure that I'd recommend to fans of Untitled Goose Game. You play as Tom, a creepy girl who's tasked with delivering packages to the people of her wacky town, which is depicted with storybook-style illustrations and a color palette limited to black, white, and red. On the surface, you're delivering packages, but the game's real story is based on Tom's tendency to peep where she shouldn't, peering into townsfolks' windows to watch their odd lives. On house is full of kids who live like dogs; another has a couple with a bizarre obsession with tickling. You never know what each window might reveal, and I quickly sympathized with (and enabled) Tom's compulsion. You also have the capacity to cause quite a bit of trouble by stomping on flowers, haphazardly snipping strings and cords, or even stealing packages and using them for your own mischievous purposes. It's a pretty short experience, completable in just a few hours, making it a nice palate cleanser between the massive releases at the end of the year.

This Devolver Digital-published game has a simple but head-turning premise. You’re a profoundly angry woman who returns to her small hometown armed with nothing but a sledgehammer, which she uses to smash everything in sight. The town is also inhabited by robots possessing human consciousnesses. Swinging the hammer can either punch holes through walls or, with enough force, reduce entire buildings to rubble. But why is she doing this? Why is she so mad? A big part of Virtue and a Sledgehammer’s allure is its fascinating and well-written tale about the protagonist’s strained relationships with her sister and mother. Learning more about their lives requires you to keep smashing, but the more you learn, the more you begin to question whether smashing everything is actually a good idea.

This bizarre indie blends fun match-3 puzzle-solving with tower defense gameplay wrapped around a funny but surreal story. The match-3 gameplay involves sliding tiles to match geographic elements like castles, trees, and rivers to collect resources that feed into the tower defense portion. Depending on how the board looks when the puzzle portion ends, you send troops (sustained by the resources you collected) to attack/defend against rival castles and gather more items; board positioning determines how well this can go. The two mechanics feed into each other to create a fun loop that grows in complexity as new mechanics are introduced. Did I mention the game is also very weird? The silly tale centers on a medieval court designating you the chosen savior to rescue their lost queen (and many other tasks), and the dumb tone adds personality to a sometimes dry genre. Titanium Court charmed and impressed us when it launched on PC earlier this year, and now console and mobile players get their chance to hold court.

Sword of the Sea is a beautiful, 2025 game about surfing through the sand atop a floating sword. It recalls Journey, the emotional 2012 PlayStation game, which makes sense as it comes from the artists and developers that worked on that game, developer Giant Squid. Giant Squid also made 2016's Abzû and 2020's The Pathless. It's a talented team and Sword of the Sea maintains that reputation. And now you can play it on Switch 2. You can read my full review of the game (though this review pertains to the PlayStation 5 version) right here.

Cities: Skylines arrived on PC more than a decade ago, but is still revered as one of the greatest modern city-builders. Even now, three years after the sequel's release, Paradox continues supporting and porting the original game. A couple years after its initial release, Cities: Skylines received a strong console port, which did an admirable job of adapting the controls to gamepads, but the Switch version was always the weakest of the bunch. As of this week, Switch 2 owners can play a less compromised version, expanding the Switch's 9-tile limit to a much larger 25-tile limit, as well as better performance and textures, better control panels, and a ton of DLC and added content. And on top of that, if you own the Switch 1 version, you get a deep discount on the Switch 2 version.

While not specifically about this new Switch 2 version, you can read our original reviews of the base PC version here, and the base console version here.

Minecraft has held its dominant spot in pop culture for so long that it's easy to forget a simple fact about it: the game is awesome. This week, it's coming to Switch 2, giving potential miners another platform to explore procedurally-generated caves in. You've certainly heard of it, and you've probably played it, but I still feel it often doesn't get the flowers it deserves in high-level critical discussions about games, despite its regular cadence of major updates. The opening gameplay loop is so satisfying that for many of my peers, whether they regularly play video games or not, it's only a matter of time before they boot up a new world again. While you can never play the game for the first time again, if you haven't checked it out in a couple years, you might be surprised by the amount of new blocks, materials, and mobs they've added in recent updates. And if you've never played before, the Switch 2 launch is as good a time as any to see what all the fuss is about.

The card game incarnation of Arkham Horror remains one of the best narrative-driven and horror-themed tabletop games around, and it's an easy recommendation if you're looking for something engaging to dive into on Halloween night. Rooted in the monsters and mysteries of the Cthulhu Mythos, this living card game is built on major core sets and expansions. But unlike a TCG, each new installment has the same cards included, fueling the cooperative adventures you'll undertake together with your fellow players. Last year Arkham Horror: The Card Game did something of a soft relaunch for a chapter 2 of its narrative, and that new core set is an ideal place to jump on  play. Players each control an individual investigator as they explore arcane and weird mysteries, confront monsters, and unfold plots of cultists, ancient entities, and forbidden lore. For fans of cosmic horror storytelling, it's an easy pick.

#4025. Nioh 3 is killing it on Steam with over double the series' highest concurrent player count

People seemingly haven't been able to stop playing Nioh 3 since the moment it came out, and everyone helped push the numbers to unprecedented heights for the series.

Nioh 3 has had a massive weekend on Steam, the type of launch you just don’t often see for Koei Tecmo games. Indeed, this has very clearly been a monumentous release for both the publisher, and developer Team Ninja.

It is also, quite visibly, the most popular Nioh release ever on PC, and it was impressive watching more and more players jump into the game over the weekend and push the numbers higher.

Nioh 3 came out swinging, breaking the series’ Steam concurrent player record immediately after lanch, with 42,822. Anyone keeping up with how well the game has been received, and how much it’s been anticipated by series fans and Soulslike players, would’ve told you that it was only the beginning.

Late on Friday, and several times on Saturday, the game continued achieving new records, setting new peak concurrent levels every couple of hours. It happened again on Sunday, when the game finally settled on its current 88,045 peak concurrent (via SteamDB).

That’s an incredibly healthy player base, but more than that, it’s more than double the previous record holder, Nioh 2, which peaked at 41,325 concurrent players in 2021. Steam players appear to be very happy with the game, too, with over 1,560 reviews and an overall Very Positive rating.

If you’re among the millions who jumped into Team Ninja’s latest, our guides offer a great place to start. These Nioh 3 gameplay tips cover a wide range of subjects; essential reading for newcomers and veterans. You should also consider changing these settings before you jump in, as it’s going to maker your life easier.

For more useful information, catch up with our list of best weapons for Samurai and Ninja, and how to easily play the game in co-op.

#4024. Nintendo Reiterates Plans For Zelda's 40th Anniversary

"We will pursue a variety of initiatives"

You can't really avoid it in the gaming space right now, but if you did somehow miss it, Nintendo is currently celebrating the 40th anniversary of the Zelda series.

Following the release of Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 this week, the firm has now issued a reminder about the series' anniversary in its latest financial results briefing. For the remainder of this year and throughout next year, it will pursue a "variety of initiatives" to celebrate the series.

It's not only focused on game releases, and fans who cherish the "earlier titles", but also merchandise, music (a worldwide concert), and of course, the Zelda movie - scheduled to arrive early next year. Here's what's on the way:

"Over the course of this year and next, we will pursue a variety of initiatives to celebrate the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda. In addition to games, we will expand opportunities for consumers to experience its world through the movie, music, character merchandise, and more.

"We will make the series even more appealing by offering different ways to enjoy it, both for those who cherish its earlier titles and for those discovering it for the first time."

You can get a recap about all the recent Zelda 40th anniversary announcements in our round up of the Zelda Direct:

Guide Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct - Every Announcement And Trailer

#4023. 8 SNES JRPGs That Reward Players for Exploring the World More Than Grinding Levels

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

When the JRPG genre was born, its progression was as basic as it gets: kill enemies, gain levels, become stronger. The in-game economy also revolved around earning gold to buy new equipment, but leveling up was the sole driver of power. Many NES and SNES JRPGs demanded some grinding, and since most battles were random encounters, you naturally did it as you moved along.

From classic Final Fantasy to Undertale, these 10 JRPGs reward understanding your enemy more than stacking up levels

Occasionally, however, games emerged that promoted more horizontal progression, focusing less on experience points or level-ups and instead rewarding players who explored every nook and cranny of the world or engaged deeply with unique mechanics introduced in each title. Today, I will explore several SNES JRPGs that reward players for venturing out into the world or leveraging a game's unique feature rather than mindlessly grinding for levels.

No better way to kick things off than with a JRPG that doesn't even feature traditional levels. Illusion of Gaia is part of what is commonly called the Quintet Trilogy, a set of action RPGs crafted with tremendous care, each bringing its own distinct flavor. In Illusion of Gaia, we control Will, who can transform into two other distinct forms at various stages of the adventure: Freedan or Shadow.

To grow stronger, you need to clear out every enemy in a given room, which grants a jewel that permanently increases the protagonist's core attributes. It's a small bit of grind, but instead of defeating monsters repeatedly, you only need to defeat each enemy once per zone. It feels far more gratifying and rewarding because you maintain a clean, consistent sense of progression whenever you choose to clear rooms.

Star Ocean never received an official Western release on the SNES. Yet, it already featured several mechanics that would become defining staples for the franchise, especially if you look at the remake Star Ocean: First Departure. In tri-Ace's JRPG, gaining levels helps because it grants SP to upgrade crafting skills, letting you synthesize equipment far more powerful than anything you can find in shops. In a sense, this rewards players for exploring system mechanics rather than mindlessly slaying mobs.

The JRPG also introduced the Private Action system to build deeper connections with party members, alongside optional character recruitments and a dynamic relationship mechanic. The more you engage with everything the world of Star Ocean has to offer, the greater your rewards will be.

Terranigma is another standout title from the Quintet Trilogy, but unlike Illusion of Gaia, it actually features a traditional leveling system. Defeating enemies yields experience points, which raise attributes on level-up. Still, because Terranigma is an action RPG, execution and player skill matter far more than raw stats, so you never need to grind endlessly just to advance through the story.

Enemies occasionally drop gems you can use to buy new equipment, items, and spells, which is where the magic of exploration takes center stage. You can convert every Magirock you discover into a spell, with more options unlocking as you progress. After casting a spell, the Magirock reverts to its base form, requiring you to slot another spell into it, which directly rewards those who seek out hidden items. On top of that, the town-building sidequests form the emotional heart of Terranigma's narrative, uncovering their full potential only for players willing to track them down.

Breath of Fire is my favorite JRPG series, and each new entry has only refined its craft. While Breath of Fire II on the SNES requires a bit of early farming, especially during the Colosseum events and when Randy joins the party, a specific mechanic will empower your party members far more than any raw level-up: the Shaman system.

After you build your own village and advance through the story, Ryu can recruit Shamans hidden across the world. Using their power, you can fuse one or more Shamans with a party member, altering their form and making them exponentially stronger. For instance, Spar, who feels somewhat underwhelming by default, transforms into an absolute powerhouse through Shaman fusion, with similar massive power spikes applying to Katt and Sten. While levels remain relevant, tracking down Shamans and executing the correct fusions provides a far greater boost to overall combat strength.

The old school villains really were some of the best, as these SNES JRPGs demonstrate.

Character progression in Final Fantasy VI works completely differently depending on who is in your active party. Certain characters like Cyan, Sabin, and Terra acquire new skills and spells simply by leveling up, but others like Edgar, Gau, and Strago require you to explore the world, purchase specialized items, and battle rare monsters. Also, if you want to min-max your stats, you'll want to hold off on leveling until you acquire Espers.

Leveling up in Final Fantasy VI only increases base HP and MP until you unlock Espers. Once acquired, each Esper grants specific attribute bonuses when you level up, letting you tailor and optimize character builds. While min-maxing is not strictly necessary for a casual playthrough, it adds a fascinating layer of depth. Additionally, during the second half of the game in the World of Ruin, the entire party-gathering mechanic hinges on world exploration if you want to re-recruit your full roster.

One of the most common praises directed at Lufia II centers on its brilliant dungeon design. The game features unique puzzle gimmicks and exploration mechanics reminiscent of The Legend of Zelda, utilizing specialized tools to solve environmental hazards. Every dungeon comes packed with secret rooms containing rare loot. It even carries a touch of Metroidvania flair, as tools acquired in later dungeons can be taken back to earlier areas to uncover hidden rewards.

Dragon Eggs are also scattered across the world and yield stat-enhancing potions, rare fruits, or powerful rings once you deliver them. Most importantly, Lufia II features Capsule Monsters that battle alongside your party. They act independently and evolve by eating items from your inventory, meaning you need a vast hoard of gear to feed your companions. Raising them isn't about grinding levels but about exploring dungeons, accumulating gold, buying items, and tracking down rare drops.

If a JRPG strikes a clean balance between combat progression and world exploration, it is Super Mario RPG. Mindless grinding is rarely necessary. And while leveling up offers significant stat boosts, grinding levels can feel overly tedious. True to its Mario roots, the game packs plenty of environmental puzzles and secrets that make exploration well worth your jumping time.

For example, expanding your maximum Flower Points requires hunting down specific hidden items across the world. You can also hunt for Frog Coins, a rare currency you can trade for powerful accessories and items. Game-changing equipment also hides off the beaten path, such as the Lazy Shell, which bestows absurd defensive stats that practically trivialize combat. It's a prime example of how vital exploration can be in shaping your party's strength.

Among the endless stream of compliments Chrono Trigger has received over the years, praise for its pacing remains one of the most common. Chrono Trigger omitted random encounters entirely, an unheard-of design choice for its era. Furthermore, the game never demanded grinding, letting you push through main-story challenges smoothly without ever looking back. That holds true right up until you acquire the Epoch.

Once you gain access to the Epoch, you can travel between eras seamlessly to visit hidden islands packed with optional dungeons and formidable bosses. These optional challenges present a far steeper curve than the main narrative, but with proper preparation and strategy, they are completely manageable. These side areas contain the absolute best endgame equipment while offering deep narrative payoffs for the party's backstories. On top of that, the game features numerous alternate endings accessible via New Game+, letting you confront Lavos at different points in time and proving that Chrono Trigger's spirit of exploration extends directly into its narrative structure.

These SNES JRPGs have stories Where the World Feels Like It’s Slowly Falling Apart Around the Player.

#4022. Love and Deepspace ushers in the Year of the Horse with a Wuxia-inspired AU multi-banner and a restaurant management mini-game

A new Love and Deepspace banner event is here with a lot of rewards to earn, and brand-new Memories for all five lads to unlock.

Love and Deepspace has kicked off the next big in-game moment and is celebrating Chinese New Year with the arrival of a new 5-Star Memory Series. This year's spring-themed banner is available now until February 27, and it comes with a host of events.

The Mortality’s Tenderness banner features five new limited-time 5-Star Memories, one each for the game’s five love interests. The theme is all about warmth, reunion, and intimacy, taking place in a Wuxia-inspired setting that's once again an alternate universe from the main story of the game.

The new memory cards are Xavier: Blades with Blossoms, Zayne: Entwined Kites, Rafayel: Carved Gemheart, Sylus: Shared Lanterns, and Caleb: Clearday Return. You can pick three of the five to focus on and further pick one to guarantee on your second 5-star pull; and you can earn wish rewards by making cumulative wishes over the course of the event.

Some of the rewards you could get include limited headwear, Limited Deepspace Wishes, and — of course — Memory-themed outfits and hairstyles inspired by the new Memories. Outside of wish rewards, the Memory Series comes with growth tasks that rewards you with in-game materials for levelling up the new cards during the event. When you reach Rank 1 for any new Memory from the banner, you’ll earn a Memory-themed outfit with a special colour that matches your chosen love interest.

Illusio returns as part of the new event, too, letting you customise the look of Kindled Moments across all five new Memories. Things you can customise include selecting the outfits and accessories for each love interest, so you can recreate Kindled Moments in your own style. As always, Kindled Moments will go back to their default look after the event ends.

There’s a new mini-game to play, too, available only during the event. It’s called Courteous Fare, a frantic but familiar restaurant management simulation that allows you to unlock a variety of rewards.

Furthermore, if you log in for 10 days throughout the event, you can unlock a new outfit set, Wealth Overflow, which can be worn by any of the love interests as well as the heroine. There are other login rewards, too, like 10 Deepspace Wishes, 10 Empyrean Wishes, His and My Outfit sets, two dynamic portrait photo poses, and loads more.

Finally, the Golden Fortune event adds even more daily log in rewards in the form of one free "shake" per day, from which you can earn a random reward of between 68 and 108 Diamonds — that adds up to a total of 1,296 Diamonds if you show up every day.

#4018. Battlefield 6's next season will speed up battle pass progression, and make it so Redsec players who don't own the game can actually make progress

Season 2 of Battlefield 6 looks to bring a host of broad, positive changes to XP, progression, audio and more.

Ahead of the start of Battlefield 6’s Season 2 next week, Battlefield Studios has shared some insight into a few of the major goals the developer has with the Season 2 patch. The game’s second season was delayed in mid-January, and the developer even brought back Battlefield Labs to test out some of the new content and features coming with the new season.

Indeed, the broader goals BF Studios shared with players in a new blog post reflect some of what Labs players already went hands-on with, while others are the result of work on long-standing issues with both the game itself, as well as free-to-play mode Redsec.

We know that Season 2 is introducing a big new map to the game, Contaminated, which the developer has been teasing. The map will indeed arrive in the first part of the season, and it’s going to do so alongside a new LTM that “introduces a new element of tactics.” A second, “high-intensity map” will debut later into the season, alongside another LTM where players battle through an underground base, in darkness.

The real meat of the blog post, however, covers the broader gameplay changes everyone will see once the new season kicks off. There’s a massive focus on player progression, especially when it concerns free-to-play Redsec players.

Challenges are being streamlined yet again, with more broad parameters that don’t require specific modes. Some, like dailies, will also allow for assists to count towards their criteria. Less restrictive challenges are welcome, but even more so is the faster battle pass progression.

BF Studios is changing the rate at which battle pass Tokens are earned from career XP, and making it so they’re earnable by playing the game normally, and by completing weekly challenges. These changes should also help Redsec players, who will also benefit from faster career and weapon XP earn rates - across both battle royale, and Gauntlet. In general, the career experience should feel more rewarding, especially for earlier ranks.

Weapon balance and recoil are two areas that will continue to evolve in Battlefield 6, it seems, and Season 2 is specifically tackling recoil patterns to make them more consistent when you compensate for them.

Movement is being adjusted with the Season 2 patch, too, though thankfully it’s limited to general feel that touches areas like vaulting, ladder transitions, and acceleration curves. You should also see better continuity and consistency between animations and feel.

Audio is getting a pass with the upcoming patch, especially when it comes to footstep and interaction audio. This also extends to something the developer has been working on improving for a while, and it has to do with how the game decides which audio tracks to prioritise in busy situations.

Tomorrow, the full Battlefield 6 Season 2 trailer will be released, while a more detailed roadmap is expected by the end of this week.

#4017. Shigeru Miyamoto Proclaims November 1 is Pikmin Day, Pikmin 4 Demo Coming To Switch 2 Soon

This morning, Nintendo shared some updates related to the Pikmin franchise and has officially claimed November 1 as Pikmin Day, starting today and moving forward presumably forever.

Aside from the announcement of Pikmin Day as a general idea, Pikmin creator Shigeru Miyamoto appeared on camera to remind everyone that Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy is coming November 12. A free demo for the game, which will include one standard level and two Dandori Academy levels, will be available on November 2.

The Switch 2 version of the game (you can read Game Informer’s Pikmin 4 review here) will have improved visuals and take advantage of the Switch 2’s mic to let you say things like “Rush” and “Go to work” to Oatchi. The Dandori Academy side of the game is essentially time trials you can practice, and then on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays, you will have one chance to post your best time. You can read more about the Switch 2 version of the game here.

Miyamoto also shared that the mobile game, Pikmin Bloom, is also getting a fairly substantial update soon with secret caves. In Bloom, players will be able to find maps that reveal caves that you can send your Pikmin into to battle and find treasure. You can also find maps for Bloom by playing Pikmin 4. Caves will be coming to Pikmin Bloom later this year.

The Pikmin Day presentation also reminded viewers that every Pikmin game is available on Switch and Switch 2, though no announcements or hints were made implying that Pikmin 1 and 2 would be coming to the Nintendo Switch Online subscription service, which includes GameCube games on Switch 2. Those games can be purchased individually on the eShop.

Finally, Miyamoto brought actress Fuka Koshiba on the presentation (best known for voicing Kiki in Kiki’s Delivery Service) to share her appreciation for the Pikmin franchise (she likes to knit Pikmin hats that she shares on social media) and introduce a Pikmin short film. In the short, a Pikmin interacts with a toad, but I won’t spoil what happens. Miyamoto promised more shorts are on the way and in the future, they will be found in the Nintendo Today app.

Unfortunately, the stream concluded without a single reference to 2017's Hey! Pikmin. I wouldn't expect it to get a port to Switch 2 anytime soon.

#4016. Call of Duty: Warzone Mode Lets You Drop a Nuke for $1 Million, But There’s a Catch

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

Season 1 of Modern Warfare 4 saw the beginning of a new era for Call of Duty: Warzone with the debut of the Zodiac map. As a Resurgence map, Zodiac is compact and blends numerous combat environments for diverse and action-packed gameplay.

Despite Warzone’s full integration with Modern Warfare 4, battle royale modes feature unique mechanics, new equipment, and a fresh set of mastery camos to work towards.

This is DualShockers' review of COD: Modern Warfare 4, covering all the ins and outs of the campaign, multiplayer, and the new DMZ Extraction Mode.

Call of Duty players will know that earning a nuke is the ultimate display of dominance. Nukes are back in Warzone, but the way you acquire one is different from what you may be used to.

In previous iterations of Warzone, to drop a nuke, you would have to complete the Champion’s Quest. To unlock the Champion’s Quest, you needed to win five Warzone matches in a row or win 30 games within a season. Meeting either of those requirements would see the Champion’s Quest contract spawn at the beginning of your next match.

After accepting the Champion’s Quest, you and your squad would have to collect three radioactive elements from around the map that were needed to assemble the nuke at a bomb site. This would also mark you on the map for the entire lobby to see. Then, you’d have to defend the nuke, as other players could come in and defuse it. If the nuke was defused, your squad was wiped out, or the nuke timer hit zero before completing all the requirements, you’d fail to detonate the nuke.

It was by no means an easy feat, and it required a lot of teamwork to get the job done. With the launch of Warzone Season 1, you can still nuke the lobby, but some of the grind has been taken out of obtaining one.

To drop a nuke on the Warzone map, Zodiac, you must be the first player to purchase it from a Buy Station for $1 million cash. This means you and your squad must work together to loot as much cash as possible, earn cash from completing contracts, eliminating bots, and more, all while staying alive to keep it in your pocket until you reach the $1 million mark.

However, you can only detonate a nuke in Zodiac via Warzone’s Rally Point game mode. Rally Point is a training ground experience that supports a maximum of 20 players. It’s designed to allow you to explore the map, try out different weapons, and take your time mastering the mechanics. A nuke can’t be purchased from Buy Stations or acquired any other way in regular battle royale matches.

Anyone can load into a match of Rally Point and begin racking up cash to purchase a nuke, as there are no other requirements to unlock it.

When you gather enough cash to purchase the nuke, you and your squad will exfil from the battlefield while you watch the map get obliterated, and the match comes to an end.

You and your squad must work together to loot as much cash as possible, earn cash from completing contracts, eliminating bots, and more, all while staying alive to keep it in your pocket until you reach the $1 million mark.

For your efforts, you will earn the Perfect End weapon blueprint for the HAN 86 assault rifle, and you can show it off across Modern Warfare 4 and Warzone multiplayer modes.

At the time of writing, it’s unknown if a nuke will be added to standard battle royale modes. Those looking to secure the ultimate bragging rights will have to master Rally Point matches, for now.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 multiplayer has arrived, and it features skill-based matchmaking, with no Open Matchmaking playlist options in sight.

#4014. Diablo 4’s next class is the Warlock, but you can sort of play it today in Diablo 2: Resurrected’s new DLC

Blizzard has officially unveiled the Warlock, the second class coming to Diablo 4 with Lord of Hatred.

Diablo 4’s segment in the big Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight was among the biggest, even if the reason most of us tuned in was somewhat spoiled earlier in the same livestream. Blizzard unveiled the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The first class, being the Paladin, is already available to play for anyone who pre-ordered the expansion, but the Warlock won’t be accessible until the expansion arrives in late April.

The Warlocks are positioned as the opposite of the Paladins, in that they don’t mind utilising forbidden knowledge, drawing on the powers of Hell itself to fight its own overlords. The Warlock is the edgy, antihero counterpart to the Paladin’s purity and devotion to the Light.

The livestream did not show off any Warlock gameplay, but Blizzard is planning a dedicated livestream to show off the new class’ gameplay, and dig deeper into its lore and abilities. That show is scheduled for March 5.

What we did get to see was our first look at Skovos, the expansion’s new region. This Mediterranean-inspired location is where the new story arc will unfold, but it’s also being positioned as the endgame destination for Diablo 4 once the credits roll.

Lord of Hatred, of course, as previously revealed, introduces two new endgame modes in War Plans, and Echoing Hatred.

War Plans lets you create a custom playlist of up to five endgame activities to target specific rewards and create your own experience. There’s a new activity tree that works with all endgame activities, and creating War Plans is how you earn progression there.

Echoing Hatred, on the other hand, is a rare event that pits you against legions of Mephisto’s minions. It’s triggered through a rare lootable item that unlocks access. It’s essentially horde mode; where you’ll face unending waves of enemies, though not without a couple of twists.

We also got a bit more colour on the expanded class skill trees, which all players will benefit from when the expansion arrives. The Talisman system, which unlocks set bonuses, was also shown off. And, of course, the return of the iconic Horadric Cube, which gives you control over Affixes.

The Anniversary Spotlight should’ve had a Year of the Warlock subtitle, because the class is also making its way to both Diablo Immortal, as well as Diablo 2: Resurrected. The showcase revealed the Reign of the Warlock DLC, which adds the aforementioned Warlock to D2R - its first new class in 25 years.

Reign of the Warlock, which is available now in D2R, also makes a few updates to the game, such as new quality of life features, the Colossal Ancients endgame encounter, updated Terror Zones and more. You also get some cosmetics in Diablo 4 if you purchase this expansion.

#4013. Yakuza Creator Toshiro Nagoshi's Studio Has Officially Shut Down, Ending Gang Of Dragon's Development With It

Nagoshi Studio, the developer led by Yakuza/Like a Dragon series creator Toshiro Nagoshi, has officially shut down, ending development of Gang of Dragon, which was revealed at The Game Awards last year. Shareholders resolved to dissolve the studio on October 31, according to a notice published in a Japanese government newspaper called Kanpo, as first reported by Gematsu.

This follows a report from Bloomberg earlier this year that said Chinese gaming megacorp NetEase Games was cutting funding to Nagoshi Studio, allowing Nagoshi to seek independent funding elsewhere. It seems he couldn't find funding, and now Nagoshi Studio is no more. NetEase helped Nagoshi found the studio in November 2021.

You can watch the Gang of Dragon reveal trailer below for a look at what the team was cooking up:

This closure follows other signals that NetEase is looking to divest from the gaming scene outside of its Chinese studios. A little over a month ago, Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture left NetEase to go independent again, just months after the launch of Romeo Is A Dead Man.

#4012. The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Master Quest DLC Leaks

If you're already familiar with the original Ocarina of Time, the remake is undoubtedly easier to beat than it was 28 years ago. Thankfully, a new DLC just leaked that might offer a more challenging experience for veteran players.

MrCheeze, a dataminer who specializes in reverse engineering, posted a list of strings to Bluesky after some digging. Pictured below, you can see several lines they uncovered that are tagged 'MQ'—listed next to Dodongo Cavern. They followed up in the comments with yet another finding: "HasMQ, IsMQModeExist, NewGameMQ, ReleaseMQ."

MQ almost certainly stands for 'Master Quest'—originally a bonus disc for Ocarina of Time, and later packaged with the 3DS launch. It's a separate mode that completely overhauls the base game's dungeons to make them more challenging. Mini-bosses are encountered earlier, optional items are made mandatory, and layouts altered, meaning that you can no longer rely on memory to progress through the game.

As broken down by @OatmealDome on X, it's currently referred to in the files as DLC, but "the data is incomplete." So far, they've only found references to MQ affecting dungeons, not the overworld. But those changes line up with the 3DS version of Master Quest. "I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly)," they said.

Nintendo SVP says remakes are as important to Nintendo as new games.

The 3DS version of Master Quest required you to beat the game before it could be unlocked, and lining up with @OatmealDome's findings, it completely mirrored the game. Enemies and bosses also dealt double damage, making it an even more challenging experience than the original GameCube version.

Series producer Eiji Aonuma previously stated in an interview with IGN that "I don't think we would announce anything specific at this time" when asked if Master Quest would be implemented in the Switch 2 remake, but these leaks at least point to Nintendo considering it. Whether MQ is actually implemented is another question entirely, as this may simply be leftover code from a scrapped idea, rather than concrete plans. It's also unclear from the leaks whether it will be a free launch, as with the 3DS version, or a paid bonus.

Master Quest was a popular request ahead of the Ocarina of Time remake's launch, so it's reassuring to see that the team are at least experimenting with the idea.

We finally got a chance to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and it's still one of the best games ever made.

#4010. 10 Abilities That Ruin Good Pokémon

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

There are some amazing Pokémon out there that are great for both playing through the game and using them in competitive battles. These Pokémon are often the go-to for those who like to play competitively.

However, there are also Pokémon that are good, but they are absolutely ruined because they have a bad ability. Think of Pokémon like Slaking, who has a high base stat total, but the fact that it has the Truant ability makes it so it can only attack every other turn.

Otherwise, this Pokémon is just loafing around. There are several Pokémon like this that would be amazing if it wasn’t for a terrible ability holding it back.

Swampert is a great Pokémon, and one my go-to starter Pokémon line in Ruby and Sapphire. It has solid stats, with it being a good attacker who only gets better when it Mega Evolves.

The only thing lacking for Swampert is its speed, as it only has 60 speed, but the rest of its stats more than make up for its lack of quickness. Unfortunately, it has two abilities that somewhat ruin it. These abilities are Torrent and Damp.

Damp just prevents explosions, and Torrent increases Swampert’s water-type moves, but only when it is low in health. Thankfully, Mega Swampert gets Swift Swim, which doubles its speed in the rain.

I mentioned it in the intro, but it needed to be an entry on this list, because Slaking is one of the all time greatest Pokémon stats-wise, but its ability makes it so it can’t do anything.

If you weren’t aware, Slaking has a base stat total of 670, which means that it rivals legendary Pokémon like Rayquaza. With power like that, Nintendo and Game Freak needed a way to make it so Slaking didn’t destroy the world, so they gave it Truant.

Truant makes it so it has to loaf around every other turn, leaving it open to attack and set-up moves. This ability absolutely destroys Slaking, making it a complete pass in most circumstances.

Regigigas is a powerhouse, and there is no denying it. With an attack stat of 160, this Pokémon dominates with physical attacks. However, it is ruined by its horrible ability, Slow Start.

Slow Start may sound like it simply slows a Pokémon down, and that is partly true, but it is worse than that. This ability makes it so the Pokémon’s speed and attack stats are both halved for the first five turns of battle.

Five turns is a ridiculously long time to have half of your attack, and it basically ruins Regigigas, as it can be defeated within those first five turns by any competent trainer. Just bring out a special attacker, and Regigigas doesn’t stand much of a chance.

A complementary Ability can turn a weak, stat-challenged Pokemon into a force to be reckoned with and here are the best.

Machamp is a fan-favorite Pokémon that is an absolute powerhouse. It rocks an overall base stat total of 505, with a high attack stat, decent defense, and decent HP. Unfortunately, it is brought down by the ability No Guard.

No Guard was the signature ability of the Machamp line prior to Generation V, and it makes it so enemy and player attacks always land. This means that accuracy suddenly doesn’t matter as both Pokémon will always hit their target.

This means that even 1-hit KO moves are guaranteed to land, and if Machamp is outsped, then it is curtains for this Pokémon. It doesn’t help too much that Machamp also has Guts, which increases its attack by 50%, but only when it has a status condition.

To be fair, Illuminate isn’t the worst ability out there, but it has absolutely no effect in battle, making it completely useless to have on a strong Pokémon. Starmie is one such Pokémon that has a useless ability.

Instead of Illuminate affecting anything in battle, it simply increases your encounter rate outside of battle. This is okay whenever you are trying to farm for a specific Pokémon, but it is otherwise useless.

It would be nice for this to be a hidden ability on Starmie instead of its primary ability alongside Natural Cure (which has a little more value). Thankfully, it gets the ability Huge Power whenever it Mega Evolves, as this amplifies its power.

Imagine that you caught a Wimpod. You stuck with it despite its flaws, raised it to level 30, and you were rewarded with it evolving into Golisopod. This is a significant power boost. After all, it has a base stat total of 530.

Unfortunately, the ability Wimp Out, which is the main ability of Wimpod, has changed into Emergency Exit. While the name of the ability has changed, the effect of the ability has not, making it so Golisopod will switch out whenever its health falls below 50%.

This ability isn’t the worst, but it does make using Golisopod a bit of a nuisance. After all, it may be a great match-up against a Pokémon you are fighting, but then it switches out because its health got too low.

From Ultra Necrozma’s stat boosts to Volo’s grueling final battle, these Pokémon encounters bend the rules to deliver memorable challenges.

Gallade is a great Pokémon that matches the 518 base stat total of Gardevoir, is psychic and fighting type, and hits like a truck with its 125 attack stat. However, the ability Steadfast is pretty pointless.

Steadfast is an ability that increases the Pokémon’s speed by one stage whenever it flinches. This is an okay ability, but it doesn’t come into effect very much, which is unfortunate since Gallade doesn’t have the best speed.

It has an 80 speed stat, which means there are a lot of Pokémon that will outspeed it. However, they have to specifically use flinching moves to make Gallade’s speed increase, and if that doesn’t happen, then the ability never gets used, making it a complete waste.

Rhyperior is a hefty Pokémon with a base stat total of 535, making it very powerful, especially with an attack stat of 140. It also boasts high defense, with a score of 130, and great health that has a score of 115. It is a tank, and it needs to be since its speed stat is only 40.

However, the worst part about Rhyperior is the ability Lightning Rod. This ability makes it so any single-target eclectic attacks are redirected to Rhyperior. Since Rhyperior is a ground-type it isn’t affected by electric attacks.

However, the only way this ability is effective is if you are doing double-battles. After all, nobody would dare bring out an electric-type Pokémon against a ground type, unless the sprinklers are on. Solid Rock does help its defences, but with those pesky x4 weaknesses, it's not going to do enough.

Archeops is coming in with a staggering 567 base stat total. This is very impressive, especially when you look at its attack and speed stats, which happen to be 140 and 110. It hits fast, and it hits hard.

Unfortunately, Archeops is a bit of a Defeatist, and by that, I mean it has the ability Defeatist. This horrible ability makes it so that the Pokémon’s attack and special attack are halved whenever its health falls below 50%.

One solid hit on Archeops that takes it below 50% health, and suddenly its attack is heavily nerfed. It wouldn’t be so bad if it could fall back on its special attack, but that is also halved.

Camerupt is a solid Pokémon with a base stat total of 460. This isn’t as strong as some of the other Pokémon on the list, but it is up there. It has both a solid special attack and attack, with them being 105 and 100.

As is the case with every Pokémon on this list, it has an ability that is pretty much useless. It gets Magma Armor, which prevents the Pokémon from becoming frozen. While this sounds good, you have to think that Camerupt is a fire type Pokémon.

If you know type effectiveness, then you know that fire-type Pokémon are super effective against ice types. In other words, nobody would dare use an ice-type move against Camerupt, even if it doesn't resist it because of its secondary ground typing. Solid Rock serves it better, though again its 4x weakness to water will usually be too much with or without it.

This list includes some Pokémon that are stronger than their evolutionary forms.
